newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Base metals see most of commodity action.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Base metals see most of commodity action.

text.p: Most of the commodity price action on Monday was in the base metals complex where threat of supply squeezes took aluminium and zinc higher, but nickel weakened despite a Canadian producers' strike.
Elsewhere coffee was lifted by concerns over nearby supplies of the arabica type bean while precious metals were featured by a sharp rise in palladium.

Zinc prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) continued to recover from the $300 a tonne drop early last week as the market continued to be concerned about the likelihood of a supply squeeze developing in September, when Chinese smelters are due to deliver large quantities of metal into LME warehouses.

The fact that premiums for nearby delivery zinc held at around $100 a tonne above three months delivery metal convinced traders that the Chinese had not yet managed to buy back, or roll forward, their commitments, or that they would have enough metal available to fulfill delivery.
Three months delivery zinc reached $1,495 a tonne, a gain of $32 from Friday.

A developing squeeze in the aluminium market, which traders said was being put on granters of August or September call options who had not covered their commitments, took the price of three months metal up to $1,747 a tonne, the highest since October 1995.
But the main focus of attention was on the premium for nearby delivery which widened to around $7 a tonne from $2 at the end of last week.
A strike at Canadian nickel producer Falconbridge's Sudbury, Ontario, mine and smelter was dismissed as an immediate threat to world nickel supplies, traders said.
Three months delivery nickel dropped $170 a tonne to $7,215 on the LME.
On the coffee market a cold air mass heading towards Brazil's coffee belt would, according to independent meteorologist Somar, be prevented from being a frost threat by the presence of cloud cover.
Coffee traders instead focused on the low level of South or Central American arabica coffee beans available to the New York market for the next couple of months.
This pushed London market September futures upto $1,670 a tonne, up $52 from Friday.
A shortage of supplies of palladium pushed the price in the London market to $239 an ounce, within $1 of June's 17 year highs.

Those highs were prompted by a six-month absencee of supplies from major world exporter Russia. Although exports had since resumed, they were not coming through in the quantities needed by the market, traders said.
